:::{#def-eigendecomposition}
#### Eigendecomposition

Let $\matr{A}$ be a $p \times p$ symmetric matrix with real entries.
An **eigendecomposition**, or **spectral decomposition**, of $\matr{A}$
is a factorization

$$
\matr{A} = \matr{Q}\matr{\Lambda}\tp{\matr{Q}}
$$

with $\matr{Q}$ a $p \times p$ orthogonal matrix (@def-orthogonal-matrix)
and $\matr{\Lambda}$ a $p \times p$ diagonal matrix (@def-diagonal-matrix).
@thm-spectral says that every such $\matr{A}$ has one.

:::

::: notes
An eigendecomposition is not unique.
For example, reordering the eigenvalues on the diagonal of $\matr{\Lambda}$,
and the columns of $\matr{Q}$ with them, gives another one,
and so does multiplying a column of $\matr{Q}$ by $-1$.
:::

{{< slidebreak >}}

:::{#exm-spectral}
#### An eigendecomposition of a $2 \times 2$ symmetric matrix

For $\matr{A} = \begin{bmatrix} 2 & 1 \\ 1 & 2 \end{bmatrix}$,
@exm-eigenvalue found the eigenvectors $(1, 1)$ for $3$ and $(1, -1)$ for $1$.
They are orthogonal (@def-orthogonal-vectors):

$$
\ba
(1, 1) \cdot (1, -1)
&= 1 \cd 1 + 1 \cd (-1)
&& \text{(definition of the dot product)}
\\
&= 0
&& \text{(multiply and add)}
\ea
$$

Each has norm $\sqrt{1^2 + 1^2} = \sqrt{2}$ (@def-euclidean-norm),
so dividing each by $\sqrt{2}$ gives two orthonormal eigenvectors
(@def-orthonormal-vectors).
Put them in the columns of $\matr{Q}$,
and the matching eigenvalues on the diagonal of $\matr{\Lambda}$:

$$
\matr{Q} = \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 1 \\ 1 & -1 \end{bmatrix}
\qquad
\matr{\Lambda} = \begin{bmatrix} 3 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix}
$$

This $\matr{Q}$ is symmetric, so $\tp{\matr{Q}} = \matr{Q}$. Then

$$
\ba
\matr{Q}\matr{\Lambda}\tp{\matr{Q}}
&= \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 1 \\ 1 & -1 \end{bmatrix}
\begin{bmatrix} 3 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix}
\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 1 \\ 1 & -1 \end{bmatrix}
&& \text{(substitute)}
\\
&= \frac{1}{2}
\begin{bmatrix} 1 & 1 \\ 1 & -1 \end{bmatrix}
\begin{bmatrix} 3 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix}
\begin{bmatrix} 1 & 1 \\ 1 & -1 \end{bmatrix}
&& \text{(collect the scalars)}
\\
&= \frac{1}{2}
\begin{bmatrix} 3 & 1 \\ 3 & -1 \end{bmatrix}
\begin{bmatrix} 1 & 1 \\ 1 & -1 \end{bmatrix}
&& \text{(multiply the first two matrices: column } j \text{ times } \lambda_j \text{)}
\\
&= \frac{1}{2}
\begin{bmatrix} 3 \cd 1 + 1 \cd 1 & 3 \cd 1 + 1 \cd (-1) \\ 3 \cd 1 + (-1) \cd 1 & 3 \cd 1 + (-1) \cd (-1) \end{bmatrix}
&& \text{(definition of matrix multiplication)}
\\
&= \frac{1}{2}
\begin{bmatrix} 4 & 2 \\ 2 & 4 \end{bmatrix}
&& \text{(multiply and add within each entry)}
\\
&= \begin{bmatrix} 2 & 1 \\ 1 & 2 \end{bmatrix}
&& \text{(multiply by } \tfrac{1}{2} \text{)}
\ea
$$

which is $\matr{A}$.

:::
